common.title: Welcome to Nodus
common.summary: Nodus is a local-first desktop workspace for research, teaching and study. Work is organised into focused vaults that share one private engine.
common.details: A vault is an independent workspace for one project, course, family or dataset. Changing the vault changes the navigation and assistant context, while the database, indexes and preserved files stay on the computer. Accounts are optional, and model-assisted features run only after a provider or local model has been configured.
common.location: Install Nodus, then open the application
steps: Download the package for macOS, Windows or Linux from the Nodus release page and complete the installer.
Launch Nodus and complete the short setup: appearance, optional Nodi assistant and the introductory tour.
Create the vault that matches the work you are starting, give it a clear name and remain on Home while you learn the layout.
tips: Use one vault per coherent project, course, family or dataset.
Start with a small set of real material that you are allowed to process.

common.title: Create and switch vaults
common.summary: Create independent workspaces and move between them without mixing their context.
common.details: Switching vaults switches projects, completely. Each one keeps its own notes, analysis and domain records. The one thing that crosses the boundary is the global Library, which can link the same source into several compatible vaults without making a second copy of it.
common.location: Application header → vault name and icon
steps: Select the current vault name in the centre of the application header, then choose the action to create a vault.
Enter a descriptive name, select the correct vault type and read the explanation of the workflow it enables before confirming.
Open the same switcher whenever you need another project; choose a vault and wait for its Home view to appear.
tips: Use explicit names such as ‘MA thesis - memory’ or ‘Biology 2026’.
Create a new vault instead of changing the meaning of a mature workspace.

common.title: Navigation and global search
common.summary: The sidebar exposes the workflow for the active vault; search retrieves material across the relevant local index.
common.details: The narrow left sidebar contains the active vault’s tools. Hover an icon to read its label. The magnifying-glass button opens search, while the vault button in the header changes workspace. Keyword search works immediately; semantic retrieval also requires an embedding model.
steps: Move the pointer over sidebar icons until the label for the section you need appears, then select it; the active icon receives the vault colour.
Open Search and enter a title, name, quotation or concept of at least two meaningful characters.
Apply a type or scope filter when available, open a result and follow its source link to the original document, record, person or note.
tips: Search for concepts as well as exact titles.
Rebuild an index from Settings if recently imported content does not appear.

common.title: Library, sources and reader
common.summary: Keep preserved originals beside clean reading copies, citations, highlights and extracted evidence.
common.details: The cross-vault Library can mirror Zotero, import RIS, BibTeX and CSL JSON, or accept files directly. Nodus preserves the original attachment and creates searchable derivatives. Compatible sources can be linked to several vaults without copying the original.
steps: Open Library and add a local file, import bibliographic data or connect Zotero.
Place the item in a collection and add useful tags; wait for extraction and indexing to finish.
Open the item, choose the clean reading copy or preserved original, then highlight passages and link the item into the active vault.
tips: Keep the preserved original for page-accurate verification.
Treat automatically extracted text and metadata as a first pass that may need correction.

common.title: AI providers and task models
common.summary: Bring your own cloud key or use compatible local models, with a different model for each task.
common.details: Nodus can be used without a model for deterministic organisation and editing. Features that generate, explain or synthesise text need a configured provider or compatible local endpoint. Provider keys are stored in the operating-system keychain, and task models let extraction, chat and reports use different choices.
common.location: Left sidebar → Settings → AI and providers
steps: Open Settings and find the AI provider section. Choose a cloud provider or enter the address of a compatible local endpoint.
Enter the required credential, use the connection test and resolve any error before continuing.
Assign a model to each available task, save the settings and test it on a small, non-sensitive source.
tips: A local model improves privacy but may require more memory and time.
Review every generated claim against its linked evidence.

common.title: Privacy, backups and recovery
common.summary: Protect local work with a verified backup and understand exactly when network services are used.
common.details: Vault databases, indexes and library files are local by default. A backup can cover every vault and the shared Library at once. Nodus reports the health of that backup, and it writes a protected recovery copy of its own before any major migration.
steps: Open Settings, choose a backup destination and enable automatic backups.
Run a manual backup, then use verification to confirm that its manifest and files are readable.
Review the privacy notice for each optional online feature before sending content.
tips: Store backups on a different physical device or a trusted encrypted location.
Sync is not a backup. It replicates your mistakes at the speed of light. Keep versioned recovery copies.

common.title: Toolkit and integrations
common.summary: Convert, protect, translate, OCR and present documents, or connect Zotero, Word, MCP clients and Nodus Server.
common.details: Toolkit holds the file utilities every vault shares. The integrations are all optional. Zotero supplies bibliographic material, Word can read selected Nodus context, MCP exposes the local tools you approve, and Nodus Server publishes a copy you choose, never the source vault itself.
steps: Open Toolkit and choose Convert, Protect, Translate, OCR Workspace or Nodus Presenter.
Select a file from disk or a compatible vault source, then review every output option and destination.
For an integration, enable only the connector you need and test it with a non-sensitive file before using project material.
tips: Permanent redaction in Protect is local and irreversible in the exported copy.
Published server spaces should contain only material intended for their readers.

vaults.name: Academic Research
vaults.tagline: Turn a scholarly corpus into traceable ideas, debates, gaps and writing.
vaults.description: The Academic vault is designed for literature reviews, theses and research projects. It links every interpretation back to a work, passage and citation while supporting discovery, synthesis and long-form writing.
vaults.audience: Researchers, doctoral candidates, students and evidence-led writers.

chapters.title: Home and research status
chapters.summary: Read the health of the corpus and jump to the most useful next action.
chapters.details: Corpus totals, recent activity, analysis progress and shortcuts, in one place. Nothing lives here: every card opens the view it summarises.
steps: Check the corpus and idea counts after importing sources.
Review processing or coverage warnings before starting synthesis.
Use Recent activity or a recommended next step to resume work.
tips: A small, carefully chosen corpus almost always analyses better than everything you own.

chapters.title: Search
chapters.summary: Search works, ideas and authors with exact and semantic retrieval.
chapters.details: Results keep their entity type and their source context, so you can tell an idea from the work it came from. Semantic search earns its keep when the corpus says something in words you would never have searched for.
steps: Enter a title fragment, author, quotation or concept.
Compare idea, author and work results rather than opening only the first hit.
Open the source record and verify the relevant passage.
tips: Use filters or a narrower query when the corpus spans unrelated fields.

chapters.title: Library and corpus
chapters.summary: Build the evidence base from Zotero or local sources and decide what belongs in this vault.
chapters.details: The Library stores bibliographic metadata, attachments and searchable text. Linking an item to the vault places it in the academic corpus; removing the link does not destroy the global source.
steps: Import or sync sources and inspect title, authors, year, identifiers and attachment status.
Link relevant items into the vault and organise them with collections and tags.
Open the reader to highlight, annotate and confirm page mappings.
tips: Resolve duplicate records before analysis so one source is not counted twice.

chapters.title: Knowledge graph
chapters.summary: See themes, ideas and typed relations as an interactive research map.
chapters.details: Nodes are research entities; edges are typed relations such as support, contrast or application. Presets and filters take you from the whole corpus down to one question.
steps: Choose a graph preset or filter by theme, author or relation type.
Select a node to inspect its evidence and immediate neighbourhood.
Open a connected source before accepting the interpretation represented by an edge.
tips: The graph is for finding questions. It proves nothing on its own.

chapters.title: Argument map
chapters.summary: Arrange claims and evidence into an explicit structure for a paper or chapter.
chapters.details: Argument maps make the role of each claim visible: thesis, support, objection, reply or evidence. Connections remain inspectable and can be reorganised as the argument develops.
steps: Create or open a map for one defensible research question.
Add claims from extracted ideas or write a clearly labelled working claim.
Connect supporting evidence, objections and replies, then check every leaf node for a source.
tips: If a claim has no evidence or inferential bridge, the map has found a writing problem early.

chapters.title: Ideas
chapters.summary: Review extracted claims, findings, methods and definitions with their exact evidence.
chapters.details: An idea is a structured interpretation of a specific passage. It records its type, its source and the excerpt that supports it, and from there it can join themes and relations.
steps: Filter by type or theme and open an idea.
Read the verbatim evidence and page reference.
Correct the label or relation when the extraction overstates the source.
tips: Prefer concise idea labels that make one testable or attributable claim.

chapters.title: Authors
chapters.summary: Compare an author’s works, ideas and position within the corpus.
chapters.details: An author profile aggregates only what the active corpus can support, which is usually less than what you think you know about them. That gap between documented stance and general reputation is the point of the view.
steps: Open an author and review works included in the corpus.
Compare their idea set and position map with adjacent authors.
Return to source passages before describing disagreement or influence.
tips: Do not infer an author’s complete position from an incomplete corpus.

chapters.title: Immersion
chapters.summary: Follow a guided, audio-capable journey through a central research question.
chapters.details: Immersion sequences evidence stations, commentary and a closing check. It orients you quickly. It does not read the sources for you.
steps: Choose an available immersion and review its duration and sources.
Move through each station, pausing to inspect quotations and context.
Complete the final question and save follow-up notes.
tips: Use headphones for audio, but keep citations visible for verification.

chapters.title: Research gaps
chapters.summary: Distinguish unanswered questions from places where the current corpus is merely incomplete.
chapters.details: A gap records the evidence you have, what is missing and where to look next. Treat it as a prompt, and remember that its strength depends entirely on how well the corpus covers the area.
steps: Open a gap and read the evidence already present.
Examine what would close the gap and whether the scope is explicit.
Search external catalogues for candidate sources, then update the gap after importing them.
tips: Phrase conclusions as ‘gap in this corpus’ until a broader search supports a field-level claim.

chapters.title: Debates
chapters.summary: Compare opposed or qualified positions without flattening their evidence.
chapters.details: Debate views group claims by stance and show the works standing behind each one. Boundary conditions and methodological differences usually matter more than the pro/con split does.
steps: Open a debate and identify the precise proposition under dispute.
Compare the strongest evidence on each side and inspect source passages.
Record qualifications or a synthesis that explains when each position holds.
tips: Papers aren't votes. Weigh relevance, method and evidential strength instead of counting heads.

chapters.title: Coverage analysis
chapters.summary: Measure how well the corpus supports important themes and questions.
chapters.details: Coverage shows you what the corpus is thick on and what it barely touches, which is how you decide what to read next and where the literature review honestly ends.
steps: Select a theme or question and inspect its linked works and ideas.
Review missing perspectives, dates, methods or populations.
Turn a weakness into a targeted search query or reading task.
tips: Coverage is relative to your project question, not a universal completeness score.

chapters.title: Hypotheses
chapters.summary: Turn patterns in the corpus into falsifiable propositions and test designs.
chapters.details: A hypothesis combines a statement, supporting ideas, risks and a proposed test. Keeping these fields separate prevents plausible speculation from masquerading as evidence.
steps: Create a hypothesis from a documented pattern or unresolved debate.
Attach supporting and contradicting ideas.
Write a result that would falsify it and outline the minimum viable test.
tips: A hypothesis that can't fail isn't one. If it explains every possible outcome, rewrite it.

chapters.title: Reading paths
chapters.summary: Order sources and ideas into a purposeful route through the corpus.
chapters.details: A path might open with the foundations, work through a debate and finish on the open questions. Every stop needs a reason to be there. Ranking alone is not a reason.
steps: Choose a learning or research objective.
Sequence foundational, contrasting and advanced sources.
Add a short purpose to each stop and revise the path as the corpus changes.
tips: Keep paths short enough to finish; branch optional depth instead of making one endless list.

chapters.title: Deep Research
chapters.summary: Generate a long-form, citation-rich report from the whole scoped corpus.
chapters.details: Deep Research runs as a queued job. It synthesises the material you scoped and returns a structured report whose every citation opens. What comes back is an auditable draft, not a finished text.
steps: Write a bounded question, choose the corpus scope and start the job.
Monitor the queue and open the report when processing completes.
Audit important claims through their citations, annotate problems and export only after review.
tips: A precise question and curated scope matter more than maximum corpus size.

chapters.title: Workspace, projects and notes
chapters.summary: Develop manuscripts and source-linked notes in one project workspace.
chapters.details: Workspace is the current home for projects, drafts and supporting notes. It keeps early observations close to their sources, then lets mature material move into a structured manuscript without losing provenance.
steps: Open Workspace and create a project for the paper, chapter or review.
Create notes with descriptive titles and link each observation to its relevant source or idea.
Organise the project outline, move reviewed material into the draft and verify every citation before export.
tips: Separate source notes, synthesis notes and final prose so their evidential status stays clear.

chapters.title: Academic settings
chapters.summary: Control Zotero, extraction, graph behaviour, models, Word, MCP and backups.
chapters.details: The usual provider and system controls, plus the ones only research needs: Zotero, extraction behaviour, citation style and the per-task models.
steps: Configure Zotero or direct imports and verify Library status.
Review text extraction, OCR, citation style and per-task model choices.
Enable Word, MCP or publishing only when needed, then verify backup health.
tips: Change one pipeline setting at a time and test it on a known source.

vaults.name: Genealogy
vaults.tagline: Reconstruct people, families and events without losing the documentary trail.
vaults.description: The Genealogy vault connects a family tree to people, life events, places, social relations, archival records and research notes. Every relationship can be reviewed against evidence.
vaults.audience: Family historians, genealogists and local-history researchers.

chapters.title: Home and research status
chapters.summary: See people, relationships, events, records and suggestions at a glance.
chapters.details: Recent work sits next to the relationship suggestions you haven't resolved yet. The ordering is deliberate: the documents should stay ahead of the tree.
steps: Review vault totals and recent changes.
Open suggested relationships before expanding the tree.
Use the Archive or People shortcuts to continue evidence entry.
tips: Record uncertain information explicitly instead of silently choosing one version.

chapters.title: Vault search
chapters.summary: Search people, events and the full text of transcribed records from one box.
chapters.details: Search crosses structured names and dates as well as OCR or transcript text. Results open the corresponding person, event or record.
steps: Search a surname, place, occupation, date or phrase from a record.
Compare entity types and spelling variants.
Open the source result and confirm the transcription against the image.
tips: Try historical spelling variants and nearby place names.

chapters.title: People and profiles
chapters.summary: Create a documented profile with names, dates, places, identifiers and linked evidence.
chapters.details: A person profile is the hub for life events, relationships, records and notes. Unknown, approximate and disputed values should remain distinguishable.
steps: Create a person with the minimum known identity fields.
Add life events with dates, places and citations rather than typing an unsupported biography.
Link records and relationships, then review duplicate or conflict warnings.
tips: Use alternate names for aliases, married names and spelling variants.

chapters.title: Family tree
chapters.summary: Navigate ancestors, descendants and partners through an evidence-led tree.
chapters.details: The tree draws the relationships you have accepted, and lets you focus, pan and zoom around them. It's a way to move through the vault. The person profile and its attached sources are what actually count.
steps: Open Family tree and select a focus person.
Expand the relevant generation or branch and inspect relationship markers.
Open a person card to verify parents, partners and children against evidence.
tips: Resolve duplicate people before merging branches.

chapters.title: Timeline
chapters.summary: Place personal and family events in chronological context.
chapters.details: The timeline brings births, marriages, residences, occupations, deaths and other events together. Filters help isolate one person, branch or period.
steps: Choose a date range or person filter.
Open an event to inspect date precision, place, participants and sources.
Add a note when chronology exposes an impossibility or ambiguity.
tips: Keep ‘about’, ‘before’ and ‘after’ date precision instead of inventing exact dates.

chapters.title: Social relations
chapters.summary: Document witnesses, neighbours, employers and other non-kin connections.
chapters.details: Genealogical evidence often travels through social networks. Typed relations preserve the role, period and documentary basis of each connection.
steps: Create or select both people.
Choose the relation type, direction and relevant dates.
Attach the record or note that supports the connection.
tips: Do not turn every shared record into a permanent relationship; capture context and confidence.

chapters.title: Map
chapters.summary: Explore residences, migrations and event locations spatially.
chapters.details: A place is a shared structured entity, so the same village is the same record every time instead of nine spellings of free text. Click a point on the map to open the events and people attached to it.
steps: Standardise a place name and coordinates.
Open Map and filter by person, branch or event type.
Follow a point to the underlying events and records.
tips: Preserve the historical place label even when adding modern coordinates.

chapters.title: Archive and records
chapters.summary: Preserve certificates, censuses, letters and photographs with transcription, OCR and links.
chapters.details: The Archive keeps primary sources apart from secondary literature, which is a distinction worth defending. Records can go into folders, be analysed for text, and link out to the people and events they document.
steps: Import a record and choose an appropriate document type and folder.
Review image orientation, OCR or transcription, metadata and source citation.
Link every identified person and event, marking uncertain identifications.
tips: Keep the unedited original image and record archive, collection and call-number provenance.

chapters.title: Secondary literature
chapters.summary: Use the shared Library for histories and methods that frame the reconstruction.
chapters.details: Books and articles go in Library. Certificates and family photographs go in Archive. Both feed notes and reports, and keeping them apart is what stops a secondary claim from quietly acquiring the authority of a document.
steps: Import relevant local histories or connect Zotero.
Link the source into the genealogy vault.
Highlight passages that clarify context, method or place history.
tips: Someone else's published tree is not a primary source, however confident it looks.

chapters.title: Genealogy Deep Research
chapters.summary: Synthesize a lineage or research question from structured records and notes.
chapters.details: Reports can combine people, events, places, archival records and secondary literature while retaining citations and uncertainty language.
steps: Ask a bounded question about a person, branch, migration or conflict.
Choose the relevant scope and start the queued report.
Audit every relationship and date in the result against the cited record.
tips: A report should preserve conflicting evidence rather than silently resolve it.

chapters.title: Research notes
chapters.summary: Keep hypotheses, transcription decisions and next searches linked to the evidence.
chapters.details: Notes provide flexible space for reasoning that does not yet belong in a person or event record. Links prevent conclusions from becoming detached from their sources.
steps: Create a note with a question-oriented title.
Link people, records and places mentioned in the note.
Separate observed facts, interpretations and next actions.
tips: Maintain a research log for negative searches as well as discoveries.

chapters.title: GEDCOM import and export
chapters.summary: Exchange structured family data while reviewing what the format cannot preserve.
chapters.details: GEDCOM is good for seeding a vault or handing data to someone else. It is not lossless: application-specific evidence, notes and media may not survive the round trip.
steps: Create a backup, then preview a GEDCOM import and its duplicates or warnings.
Map or review people and relationships before committing.
After export, open the file in a second tool and verify names, dates and links.
tips: A GEDCOM export is not an archival backup. It never was.

chapters.title: Genealogy settings
chapters.summary: Configure OCR, Library, maps, models, integrations and backups.
chapters.details: Extraction and optional analysis are configured here. The genealogy database itself stays local, whatever you enable.
steps: Choose OCR and transcription defaults suitable for the records.
Review provider and model choices before analysing sensitive documents.
Enable automatic backups and verify a restore point.
tips: Living-person data deserves stricter sharing and provider choices.

vaults.name: Databases
vaults.tagline: Build approachable relational datasets, inspect quality and analyse patterns.
vaults.description: The Databases vault provides typed tables, relations, formulas, rollups, views, search, analysis and grounded data chat without requiring a separate database server.
vaults.audience: Researchers, collections teams and anyone whose project has outgrown a spreadsheet.

chapters.title: Home and database catalogue
chapters.summary: Create, open and monitor the databases in a vault.
chapters.details: Every database in the vault, with its row count and a way straight into search, analysis or data chat.
steps: Create an empty database or import an existing CSV.
Give the database a specific name and description.
Open it from the catalogue or sidebar.
tips: Use separate databases for distinct entity types, then connect them with relations.

chapters.title: Columns and field types
chapters.summary: Model text, numbers, dates, options, files, relations, formulas and AI-assisted outputs explicitly.
chapters.details: Typed fields are what make filtering, validation and analysis trustworthy. A sheet of ambiguous strings will let you compute almost anything, including nonsense. Change the schema when the meaning of the data changes, not to make one awkward import fit.
steps: Add a column and choose the narrowest useful field type.
Name it in plain language and configure options, precision or validation.
Test the field on several records before bulk import.
tips: Do not encode several facts in one text column if they must be filtered separately.

chapters.title: Rows and record detail
chapters.summary: Edit records in the table or open a full record card with attachments and long fields.
chapters.details: Each row is a record. The detail view makes dense schemas easier to inspect and supports file attachments and extended content.
steps: Add a row and fill its identifying field first.
Edit compact values inline; open the record for long text, files or a complete audit.
Review required or invalid values before leaving the record.
tips: Choose one stable field as the human-readable record title.

chapters.title: Relations, formulas and rollups
chapters.summary: Connect records and calculate derived values without copying data.
chapters.details: A relation links a row to records in another database. A rollup summarises those related values. A formula computes a deterministic output from the current record, and only from the current record.
steps: Create a relation column and choose its target database and cardinality.
Link existing records rather than retyping their names.
Add a rollup or formula, then test null values and edge cases.
tips: Prefer relations over duplicated text when the referenced entity can change.

chapters.title: Table, gallery and saved views
chapters.summary: Present the same records in layouts and filters suited to different tasks.
chapters.details: A view stores layout, visible fields, filters and sort order. The rows underneath are the same rows, so a catalogue, a review queue and a fieldwork view can sit on one database without any of them being a copy.
steps: Create or switch to Table or Gallery.
Choose visible fields and configure filter groups and sort order.
Save the view with a task-oriented name.
tips: Keep one unfiltered audit view so hidden records are never mistaken for missing data.

chapters.title: Filter, sort and bulk actions
chapters.summary: Narrow records with explicit conditions and apply reviewed changes efficiently.
chapters.details: Filters combine conditions and sorts fix a stable order. Bulk operations are fast enough to do real damage before you notice, so preview or back up first.
steps: Add a filter condition, operator and value; group conditions deliberately.
Add one or more sort keys and check how blanks are ordered.
Select records, preview the bulk action and confirm only the intended fields.
tips: Export or back up before irreversible bulk changes.

chapters.title: CSV import and export
chapters.summary: Bring in existing tabular data and export CSV, XLSX or JSON.
chapters.details: Import shows you the headers and the inferred types before it writes a single row. Export honours the database and format you picked, though relations and files are represented differently depending on which format you choose.
steps: Clean obvious duplicate headers, then open Import and preview encoding and delimiter.
Map each source column to a field and review inferred dates, numbers and options.
After import, check row count and samples; before export, choose the scope and target format.
tips: Keep the original import file unchanged as provenance.

chapters.title: Cross-database search
chapters.summary: Find database names and matching content inside rows.
chapters.details: One box, every database in the vault. Results carry enough record context that you open the right row first time.
steps: Enter a distinctive name, identifier or phrase.
Use database grouping to disambiguate similar records.
Open the row and verify the value in context.
tips: Normalise identifiers and names to improve reliable retrieval.

chapters.title: Analysis and charts
chapters.summary: Inspect distributions, missing values, summaries and visual patterns.
chapters.details: The statistics and charts are deterministic and run straight off the selected database. Model-assisted reports are optional, and any that are worth reading will name the fields and the population they used.
steps: Choose a database and review row count, field completeness and detected types.
Select a categorical or numeric field for an appropriate chart.
Investigate outliers and missingness in the underlying rows before interpreting a pattern.
tips: A chart inherits every weakness of the schema and the data-entry rules behind it.

chapters.title: Data chat
chapters.summary: Ask grounded questions about a selected database and receive inspectable summaries.
chapters.details: Answers are scoped to the rows in front of you, not to what a model happens to know about the topic. Replies can include computed summaries and charts. Check anything that matters against the deterministic analysis before you rely on it.
steps: Select the target database.
Ask a precise question that names the measure, grouping and population.
Inspect cited or referenced records and reproduce critical totals in Analysis or export.
tips: Ask for assumptions and missing-data treatment explicitly.

chapters.title: AI-assisted columns
chapters.summary: Classify or summarise records into a new field under human review.
chapters.details: An AI column runs one instruction you define over fields you choose. What it writes is a proposal, and it can shift when the model or the prompt changes.
steps: Create an AI-assisted field and define its input columns and expected output format.
Run it on a small sample and refine the instruction.
Review results before processing the full set and record the model configuration.
tips: Use deterministic formulas for calculations; reserve AI fields for interpretive tasks.

chapters.title: Database-linked notes
chapters.summary: Document definitions, cleaning decisions and interpretations beside the records.
chapters.details: Notes can link to databases and rows, providing an audit trail for decisions that do not fit in the schema itself.
steps: Create a note for a method, issue or finding.
Link the affected database or records.
Record the decision, date and consequence for later analysis.
tips: Maintain a data dictionary and change log from the beginning.

chapters.title: Database settings and safety
chapters.summary: Control import behaviour, models, integrations and recoverable storage.
chapters.details: Local database maintenance sits here alongside the shared model, MCP and backup controls.
steps: Review provider and model choices for analysis and AI columns.
Test MCP access with a read-only client before exposing write operations.
Enable automatic backups and export critical datasets periodically.
tips: Treat schema migrations and bulk edits as high-risk changes deserving a backup.

vaults.name: Study
vaults.tagline: Organise a course and turn your own materials into grounded practice.
vaults.description: The Study vault keeps subjects, schedules, notes, imported materials, recordings, concepts, questions and spaced review within one private learning workspace.
vaults.audience: University and lifelong learners managing substantial course material.

chapters.title: Home and study plan
chapters.summary: See courses, materials, upcoming exams, review load and recommended next steps.
chapters.details: Organisation and learning progress in one screen. The detailed subject and review views still hold the real state.
steps: Check upcoming assessments and scheduled study sessions.
Review new material and due review counts.
Open the recommended action or a recent note to continue.
tips: Plan from deadlines backwards and keep review sessions small and frequent.

chapters.title: Courses, subjects, folders and topics
chapters.summary: Build a hierarchy that keeps each subject’s materials and AI context separate.
chapters.details: Course, then subject, then folder, then topic, then note. A subject's colour and icon follow it everywhere: into the schedule, into search, into the learning views.
steps: Create the course or degree and add its subjects.
Assign a colour and icon, then create only the folders and topics you will use.
Move or create notes and materials at the most specific useful level.
tips: Don't build empty levels. If the structure is costing you more than it saves, flatten it.

chapters.title: Schedule
chapters.summary: Lay subjects across days and time blocks.
chapters.details: Schedule is the recurring shape of your week, in your subjects' own colours. Anything with a specific date belongs in Calendar.
steps: Choose the active course and week pattern.
Add subject blocks to the correct day and morning or afternoon slot.
Review collisions and use Calendar for individual deadlines or exceptions.
tips: Leave some blocks empty. A schedule with no slack survives exactly one bad week.

chapters.title: Calendar and reminders
chapters.summary: Plan classes, deadlines, study sessions and exams with local reminders.
chapters.details: Events can carry a type, icon, link and reminder. Optional calendar export or connection should be reviewed before sharing details outside Nodus.
steps: Create an event with a clear title, type, date and time.
Link it to a subject, material or note and choose a reminder.
Use month or agenda views to rebalance crowded periods.
tips: Schedule the preparation sessions, not only the final deadline.

chapters.title: Workspace search
chapters.summary: Search notes, materials, transcripts, questions and exams in one local index.
chapters.details: Keyword and semantic retrieval return exact pages or timestamps where available.
steps: Enter an exact phrase or concept.
Filter by subject or content type.
Open the page, note or transcript timestamp that supports the result.
tips: Search your own misconceptions and questions, not only official terminology.

chapters.title: Materials and focused reading
chapters.summary: Import PDFs, documents, slides, EPUBs and audio into the course hierarchy.
chapters.details: Nodus extracts searchable text while preserving the original. Annotations and links connect materials to notes and learning objects.
steps: Import a file and assign its subject, folder and topic.
Wait for extraction, then open the clean copy or preserved original.
Highlight and annotate key passages; create a linked note for synthesis.
tips: Prefer active notes and questions over highlighting entire pages.

chapters.title: Recordings and local transcripts
chapters.summary: Record or import audio, transcribe with local Whisper and jump to exact timestamps.
chapters.details: Recordings organise by subject and link to notes. Transcribing locally means classroom audio never reaches a provider, which is usually the deciding factor.
steps: Start a recording with permission or import an existing audio file.
Choose local transcription and review the resulting speaker or text segments.
Click a transcript line to replay the exact moment and link important segments to a note.
tips: Follow institutional consent rules before recording any class or person.

chapters.title: Study chat
chapters.summary: Ask questions grounded in one subject’s materials and citations.
chapters.details: One subject at a time, so last term's material can't leak into this term's answer. Every citation opens the note, page or transcript it came from.
steps: Select the correct subject and check the included sources.
Ask for an explanation, comparison or quiz at an appropriate level.
Open the cited evidence and correct any unsupported statement.
tips: Ask the tutor to question you before explaining when practising recall.

chapters.title: Study ideas
chapters.summary: Review concepts extracted from your own notes and materials with verbatim evidence.
chapters.details: Ideas capture definitions, mechanisms and relationships while retaining the subject and source context.
steps: Filter ideas by subject or topic.
Open one and read its evidence and related ideas.
Correct or merge duplicate concepts before using them for questions.
tips: A concise concept with one clear relation is easier to learn than a paragraph label.

chapters.title: Study graph
chapters.summary: Explore concepts and typed connections as a subject map.
chapters.details: Supports, contrasts, causes and applications, drawn between the concepts from your own material. The concepts sitting alone with no edges are usually the ones you have not understood yet.
steps: Choose one subject and an overview or topic focus.
Select a node and explain its outgoing relations in your own words.
Open evidence for uncertain edges and repair the underlying idea if needed.
tips: Redraw a small part from memory after exploring it.

chapters.title: Question bank, tests and exams
chapters.summary: Build approved questions from specific source excerpts.
chapters.details: Questions organise by subject, topic, type and difficulty. Anything generated stays a draft until you approve it, and it carries the excerpt that justifies its answer while it waits.
steps: Create manually or generate from selected material.
Review wording, answer, distractors, explanation and source excerpt.
Approve the item, then assemble it into a practice test or exam.
tips: Reject ambiguous questions even if the expected answer is technically present.

chapters.title: Flashcards and spaced review
chapters.summary: Run focused review sessions and rate recall honestly.
chapters.details: Review can reuse approved content or generate a bounded session. Ratings influence when material returns.
steps: Choose subject, scope, session type and length.
Answer before revealing the back or explanation.
Rate recall based on retrieval quality, not familiarity after seeing the answer.
tips: Twenty minutes a day beats a five-hour session on Sunday, every time.

chapters.title: Study Research
chapters.summary: Create an extended study brief grounded in selected course content.
chapters.details: A study brief builds explanations and citations around one learning question, using your course material. It does not go looking on the open web unless you send it there.
steps: Ask a clear question and choose the subject or source scope.
Start the report and wait for the queued task to complete.
Read actively, open citations and turn key sections into your own questions.
tips: Use a brief as a map back into the material, not as a replacement for it.

chapters.title: Notes
chapters.summary: Write free-form notes alongside structured course content.
chapters.details: Notes can link to subjects, topics, materials and ideas. They support scratch work, summaries and reflection without losing context.
steps: Create a note under the relevant subject or topic.
Use headings and links to separate source notes from your interpretation.
Review and convert important statements into questions or ideas.
tips: Write a short retrieval summary before reopening the source.

chapters.title: Study settings
chapters.summary: Control tutor models, local transcription, reminders, privacy and backups.
chapters.details: This is where the line between the local learning tools and the optional providers is drawn, in writing.
steps: Choose the model for tutoring and generation, or configure a local endpoint.
Enable local Whisper and review microphone permissions.
Check reminder behaviour, AI policy and automatic backups.
tips: Do not upload copyrighted or sensitive course material to a provider without permission.

vaults.name: Teaching
vaults.tagline: Plan courses and assess transparently without outsourcing judgement.
vaults.description: The Teaching vault connects courses, groups, materials and schedules to reusable questions, rubrics, exams and defensible gradebooks. AI may help create teaching content but never evaluates students.

chapters.title: Home and academic-year overview
chapters.summary: Resume the current course and monitor groups, rubrics, exams and gradebooks.
chapters.details: Shortcuts and recent activity, with every assessment object still attached to the subject and academic year it belongs to.
steps: Confirm the active academic year and course.
Review group, rubric, exam and gradebook totals.
Open the most relevant recent item or start destination.
tips: Archive completed years rather than reusing their assessment objects silently.

chapters.title: Courses and subjects
chapters.summary: Define the academic-year structure that materials and assessment will reference.
chapters.details: Subjects keep consistent names, colours and schedules wherever they appear. The course above them is what planning and reporting group by.
steps: Create the academic year and course.
Add subjects with clear codes, names, colours and teaching load.
Review that groups, materials and assessment objects point to the correct subject.
tips: Keep historical subjects unchanged after grades are published.

chapters.title: Groups and private rosters
chapters.summary: Keep class lists attached to the right subject and year.
chapters.details: Roster data stays local and never enters an AI workflow. Group views exist to help you organise a class. They do not exist to profile one.
steps: Create a group and choose its subject and academic year.
Add students manually or import the approved roster format.
Review identifiers and duplicates, then restrict exports to the minimum necessary data.
tips: Never paste names, grades or student answers into an AI prompt.

chapters.title: Timetable
chapters.summary: Arrange recurring teaching slots with subject identity and location.
chapters.details: Timetable is the weekly pattern. Calendar is every specific date, deadline and exception to it.
steps: Choose the active year and week layout.
Add class blocks with subject, group, time and room.
Check collisions and add one-off changes to Calendar.
tips: Record the time zone for remote or cross-campus teaching.

chapters.title: Calendar
chapters.summary: Plan sessions, deadlines, exams and reminders.
chapters.details: Dated events can link back to courses, subjects and assessment objects, keeping preparation and delivery together.
steps: Create an event with type, date and related subject.
Add a local reminder and a link to the relevant material or exam.
Review month and agenda views for workload conflicts.
tips: Add moderation and feedback deadlines, not only student-facing dates.

chapters.title: Teaching materials
chapters.summary: Organise source files and classroom resources by subject and unit.
chapters.details: Materials can feed question and rubric drafting. Nothing generated leaves this stage without a teacher reading it.
steps: Import or create a material and assign subject, topic and audience.
Review extraction and preserve the original file.
Link the material to sessions or use a selected scope when drafting questions.
tips: Check licensing before distributing third-party material.

chapters.title: Recordings
chapters.summary: Keep permitted class recordings and transcripts attached to the course.
chapters.details: Transcribing locally keeps the audio where it is. Whether you may record at all, and for how long you may keep it, is a question for your institution's policy and the people in the room.
steps: Confirm consent and choose the correct subject before recording or import.
Transcribe locally and review errors.
Link useful segments to teaching notes or materials, then apply the retention policy.
tips: A good pedagogical reason is not consent.

chapters.title: Teaching chat
chapters.summary: Discuss a course topic with selected teaching materials as the evidence base.
chapters.details: Teaching chat explains, compares and drafts learning content from the subject you choose. Rosters, grades, submissions and anything that identifies a student never go into it.
steps: Choose the subject and inspect which materials are included in the conversation scope.
Ask for a bounded explanation, outline or activity and state the intended level.
Open the cited material, correct unsupported statements and move only reviewed content into a teaching resource.
tips: Start a new conversation when the subject or intended audience changes.

chapters.title: Teaching ideas
chapters.summary: Review concepts extracted from course materials before reusing them in activities or assessment.
chapters.details: Ideas keep short concepts and relationships attached to their supporting passage. They provide a reusable layer between raw materials and teacher-reviewed outputs.
steps: Filter ideas by subject or source and open one relevant concept.
Read the supporting passage and correct an over-broad label or relationship.
Use reviewed ideas as inputs for an explanation, question or unit activity.
tips: Keep one central concept per idea so later reuse stays precise.

chapters.title: Teaching graph
chapters.summary: Explore course concepts and their typed relationships as a visual map.
chapters.details: Prerequisites, contrasts and orphaned concepts become visible quickly. What you are looking at is the material in this vault, which is neither a curriculum standard nor a substitute for knowing your subject.
steps: Choose a subject and an overview or topic focus.
Select a node and inspect its immediate relationships and evidence.
Use gaps or weak connections to revise materials, an explanation or a unit sequence.
tips: Use the graph to ask better planning questions, not as an automatic curriculum.

chapters.title: Question bank
chapters.summary: Create reusable questions by subject, topic, type and difficulty.
chapters.details: Draft questions yourself, or from selected teaching material. Anything a model writes stays unapproved until you say otherwise, and none of it is ever used to evaluate a student.
steps: Create a question or generate a draft from an explicit material scope.
Review wording, expected answer, marking guidance, difficulty and accessibility.
Approve and tag the question before adding it to an exam.
tips: Maintain parallel items and review for cultural or linguistic bias.

chapters.title: Rubrics
chapters.summary: Define weighted criteria and achievement levels before marking.
chapters.details: Criteria, performance descriptors and weights are kept apart so each can be edited without disturbing the others. Publish or lock a version and the basis of the assessment stops moving underneath you.
steps: Create a rubric for a subject and assessment task.
Add distinct criteria, weights and observable descriptors at each level.
Validate the total, pilot on sample work and publish the approved version.
tips: Describe observable performance, not personality or presumed effort.

chapters.title: Exam builder and print export
chapters.summary: Compose an exam from approved questions with a live printable preview.
chapters.details: Sections, points, instructions and answer keys all live in the builder, with the printable preview updating as you go. Export produces a clean paper. You decide what is on it.
steps: Create an exam with subject, duration, instructions and total points.
Add approved questions, organise sections and inspect pagination in the preview.
Generate the student paper and solution copy, then proofread both before printing.
tips: Check that points, time and cognitive demand align with the published plan.

chapters.title: Gradebooks and assessment plans
chapters.summary: Apply transparent weighting rules without turning every blank into zero.
chapters.details: The rules come from a published assessment plan, and a blank is never silently a zero: missing, excused and not-yet-entered stay three different things. No model grades or profiles a student, at any point.
steps: Create or select the approved assessment plan and verify weights.
Create the gradebook for the correct group and enter or import marks.
Review missing-value semantics, calculations and outliers before publishing or exporting.
tips: Keep an audit trail for manual overrides and moderation decisions.

chapters.title: Units and learning design
chapters.summary: Plan outcomes, units and aligned activities in the course structure.
chapters.details: A unit ties intended learning to ordered material and to the assessment that follows. They work best when the boundary is clear and the outcome is something you could actually watch someone do.
steps: Open Units and create a unit under the correct course or subject.
Add the intended outcomes, sequence and links to the materials that support each stage.
Connect appropriate questions, rubrics or exams, then review the alignment before teaching starts.
tips: Use observable learning outcomes that can be checked without profiling a student.

chapters.title: Privacy and responsible AI
chapters.summary: Use AI for teaching content only; keep rosters, marks and student answers out of models.
chapters.details: There is a hard boundary around student data, and Nodus enforces it rather than trusting you to remember. Calculations are deterministic and local, judgement stays yours, and the optional models only ever draft non-personal teaching material.
steps: Open Settings, configure only the providers needed for content preparation and read the teaching AI boundary.
Use only non-student course material for optional generation; never include names, marks, submissions or behavioural observations.
Verify backups, local access controls and export destinations before adding a live roster.
tips: If the task evaluates, predicts or profiles a student, it doesn't go to a model. No exceptions.
